in_text_mentions: PG occurs most commonly on the lower legs with preference for the pretibial area [Fig. 1 &2]. PG has been reported on other sites of the body as well, including breast, hand, trunk, head and neck, and peristomal skin [Fig. 3 &4]. Extracutaneous manifestations include involvement of upper airway mucosa, eye [9-12], genital mucosa [13], sterile pulmonary neutrophilic infiltrates [14] or spleen infiltrates [15], and neutrophilic myositis [16]. Sterile cortical osteolysis has been observed adjacent to PG ulcers as another extracutaneous manifestation of the disease [17].

The ulcer starts as a follicular pustule with rapid growth, tissue necrosis and enlargement of the area. The surrounding skin is erythematous with infiltration end oedema. The ulcer borders are typically undermined and violaceous or bluish [Fig. 1]. The ulcers develop a purulent cover, which rapidly becomes malodorous due to secondary infection. A strong sensation of pain often is associated to PG [1,2,10].

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 5 panels (A, B, C, D, E). A: Clinical photo of a human patient showing mucocutaneous pyoderma gangrenosum with necrotic/crusted ulceration and nasal bridge collapse, consistent with severe mucocutaneous PG. B: Clinical photo showing full-thickness ulcerations with undermined borders, a hallmark of pyoderma gangrenosum, on the right posterior shoulder and back. C: Clinical photo of necrotic ulcerations with purulent drainage on the right lateral neck and shoulder, consistent with pyoderma gangrenosum complicated by secondary infection. D: Clinical photo demonstrating ulcerations with violaceous, undermined borders on the left lateral neck and shoulder, a classic presentation of pyoderma gangrenosum. E: Clinical photo showing extensive ulcerative lesions with exposed underlying tissue, demonstrating the depth and severity of disseminated pyoderma gangrenosum on the right posterior shoulder.
